02 · 0:49Your agent vs. an always-on agent 截图 s02

  • Runs in your terminal ｜ Runs on a server, so it survives crashes, deploys, and a closed laptop
  • Uses your laptop ｜ Has its own cloud computer: a small virtual machine with a desktop, browser, and files
  • Remembers only the messages list ｜ Saves its state, memory, and skills, and summarizes old messages
  • Prints every model reply ｜ Only messages you when it calls a send tool, so it can stay quiet
  • Starts when you type ｜ Starts on events: your messages, schedules, Slack, phone calls, finished work
  • Does one task, then exits ｜ 跨会话持续工作（右列末行被遮挡）

Part 2 · What changed in the models

07 · 6:20Six new model capabilities 截图 s08

  • 1. Work for hours — follow complex instructions the entire time
  • 2. Hand off to helpers — each helper with a fresh context, total work isn't limited by one context window
  • 3. Use real tools — a shell, files, a browser, and app APIs through MCP: the same tools you use on your computer
  • 4. Use a computer — look at a screen and click, use apps that have no API
  • 5. Keep knowledge in files — Skills and memories are stored as plain files that the agent reads and updates itself
  • 6. Learn by watching — show it how you do a task on its computer, it saves the steps as a skill it can reuse

11 · 12:19The agent's computer 截图 s12

  • 标题行：A Firecracker virtual machine · one per user · saved to disk when idle（A Linux (Debian) container, kept running by a supervisor）
  • File server — Files, app connections, live desktop view
  • Command runner — Shell commands, files, screenshots, clicks
  • Screen 1 — A virtual display with its own Chrome；Screen 2, 3, … — One more screen per active agent
  • 黑条：Files, installed tools, and browser logins all stay between sessions
  • Going to sleep（A few minutes after the last activity, never mid-turn）：1. Files sync to cloud storage 2. Memory and disk are saved as a snapshot 3. The machine stops
  • Waking up（On the next tool call）：1. The snapshot is restored in place 2. Logins and installed tools are still there 3. Conversation state comes from the server

13 · 14:06Why the agent runs on the server 截图 s13

  • Thin client, thick server ／ Close your laptop and the work keeps going ／ Easily move between your computer and phone
  • Ship code without App Store review cycles ／ Offload heavy work to the server
  • Agent loop is entirely decoupled from app code ／ Easier to scale with hyper growth ／ Agents that work for months can't be on device

论证 agent 必须跑在服务端：瘦客户端厚服务端。

[14:07] The reason agent runs on the server is uh a pretty common practice in computing where you want to have kind of a thin client and a thick server. And computing has kind of oscillated between these things over the years. But for example, a few good reasons for this is let's say you need to push an update to the, you know, the agent code. It would, you know, kind of suck if you had to push an app store update just to get that code out there versus just pushing a bunch of server updates very quickly. Um, also sometimes you need to do heavy computation work, you know, like transcription or image generation or something. And that's probably going to be faster on a server than on device depending on uh what the devices are.
[14:44] Um, and you know, it's there's very established ways that we know how to scale servers, especially with variable traffic and variable growth. Um, but the most critical thing here is that if you put the agent loop on the virtual machine, then you can't shut down the virtual machine independently from the uh from the agent server. 15 · 15:26What happens when you hit send 截图 s16

Notifications only say "something changed." The database always has the real data.

  • ① Sending：Your app shows the message right away → It saves the message locally with a unique ID → The server drops any ID it has already seen（Unique IDs make retries safe）
  • ② The turn：The message joins the conversation's queue → The agent runs one turn: model, tools, repeat → 黑条 Every step is saved to the database（One turn at a time per conversation）
  • ③ Watching：The server sends a tiny "something changed" signal → Every open app gets the signal → Each app fetches the new messages（The signal carries no data, so losing one is harmless）
  • ④ Ordering：Every update has a sequence number → Apps apply updates in order: 41, 42, 43 → If one is missing, reload from the database

发消息全链路协议：客户端生成唯一 ID，服务端去重；每会话一 turn、每步落库；通知是无数据空信号；客户端按序号应用、缺号重拉。

16 · 16:17Durable workflows vs. job queues 截图 s17

What happens when a server crashes in the middle of a turn

  • Job queue（starts over）：Step 1 → 2 → ×3 crash → restart → 重做 1、2 再跑 3-5（Redoes finished work）
  • Durable workflow（picks up where it stopped）：crash 后 resume → 直接从 Step 3 继续（No repeated work）
  • Resume from any point：Every step is recorded, so a new server picks up from the last one
  • Safe retries：Steps are written so running one twice does no harm. That's called idempotent
  • Built in, open source：Timers, cancellation, and health checks come with engines like Temporal

Grok Bot 选 durable execution 的理由：崩溃从断点续、步骤幂等、Temporal 类引擎内置定时器/取消/健康检查。

逐字稿（peterp.me 转录，内联时间戳）

[16:17] list. And so, uh, the like underlying infrastructure primitives to think about here, um, is a workflow versus a job queue. And the main difference here is with a job queue, let's say you're kind of going along on steps, you ask your agent to go and do some kind of complicated task, uh, and it's making its way from step one to step two to step three, but then for some reason there was an infrastructure issue. Um, there was some problem with a normal queue. If that crashes and you go to restart it, well, now you have to replay steps one, two, and three, which is obviously that that could be pretty problematic. So, what you really want here is you want a durable workflow, which means that it's safe for you to actually retry that. And when you retry after a failure, it picks right up on step three. And this is like kind of a solved problem in some ways in distributed systems and in infrastructure. So, we use an open source uh tool called Temporal, which is interesting to look into if you're if you're curious, so that we don't have to rebuild a lot of this very complicated stuff from scratch. Of course, you still

24 · 25:12Tips for designing agent tools 截图 s25

  • Don't add or remove tools between turns. If a tool can't be used right now, have it return a clear error
  • Keep each tool's description and schema under 4,000 characters
  • Use a dedicated tool for saving state instead of shell commands, so reviewers can see what's changing
  • Write errors that say what to do next: "The computer is asleep. Use Shell or Read to wake it, then try again."

25 · 26:28How we keep it safe 截图 s27

  • Automatic review — A separate model checks risky actions before they run. If it blocks one, you get an approval request. No answer in 15 seconds means blocked
  • Track the source — Text from emails and webhooks is labeled untrusted. Memories are treated as information, not instructions
  • Asks first — It won't email or message people unless you asked it to. New routines need your OK
  • Keep secrets hidden — Passwords go into environment variables, never to the model. Actions on your own laptop need your approval

四层安全：独立模型审批、来源打标、先问再做、密钥隔离。

26 · 27:46Keep the start of the prompt the same 截图 s28

  • 紫框 Stays the same until the next summary：Tool definitions / System prompt, including a snapshot of memory and routines / First message: environment details and a list of tool names → Identical on every call, so the provider can reuse its cached work
  • 灰框 Conversation history：New messages are only ever added at the end → Becomes part of the reusable start of the next call
  • 橙框 Newest message：The time, short notes on anything that changed, then your message → The only part that's new on each call
  • 注释：Providers charge less and respond faster when the start of a prompt matches a recent one

[27:47] about prompt caching. Um, this is a good example of why it's really important. So if you think about when you're working with a coding agent or any agent, most of the tokens used are actually ideally cached tokens because you're sending it a conversation and then you're doing a change. You're you're adding one more message and then you're basically resending the entire conversation over again. So if you look at the pricing for models, there's huge discounts of course on if a token is cached and you want to keep them in the cache window as long as possible. And so a way to do this is you try to keep the tool definitions, the system prompts, all of this information as static as possible between different calls so that you don't break the cache and then have to pay for the uncashed tokens every single time. So if you have that fixed part at the top, then you know when you get down to the bottom and you only have the newest message that comes in, that's the only delta that you're paying the uncashed tokens for.

31 · 34:29Training the model for the product 截图 s34

  • 📖 Pre-training — language, code, and general knowledge
  • 🎓 Supervised fine-tuning — learns the harness from examples: the tools and their formats / when to send a quick reply / what an ideal response looks like
  • 🏆 Reinforcement learning — real agent tasks: following long instructions / using skills and memories / clicking the right spot (grounding) / working with other bots
  • 💬 Main agent: fast replies（秒回）｜ ⏱ Helpers: long tasks（稳定跑几小时）

Then you have supervised fine-tuning where you're teaching the model how to behave uh in a certain way maybe as a chat assistant or as an agent.
